c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.text: As a costume designer, describe the costumes you would use for the Johnstone and Lyons families to communicate the social class divide to the audience.
c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed description of contrasting costumes with clear justification linked to class. E.g. The Johnstones would wear home-knitted, patched, and well-worn clothing in muted colours to show poverty. Mrs Johnstone’s wide-skirted dress and flat shoes show she is practical and cannot afford luxuries. The Lyons family would wear well-tailored suits, polished shoes, and high-quality materials to show wealth. Mrs Lyons’ high heels show she does not have to do physical work. The colour contrast (red for Johnstone/Labour vs blue for Lyons/Conservative) would communicate political affiliations.
Lower band (1-2): Basic description with limited justification. E.g. Poor family in old clothes, rich family in nice clothes.

c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.text: Explain how an actor playing Mrs Johnstone might use vocal skills to show her reluctance as she agrees to give one twin away.
c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation of vocal techniques with clear effect. E.g. The actor could use a trembling, quiet volume to show the emotional weight of admitting she cannot provide for her children. A slow pace with pauses would communicate her reluctance and pain. A falling pitch at the end of each phrase would highlight her helplessness — she has no choice. A Liverpool accent would ground her in the working-class community and remind the audience of the social context. Her tone could crack as she looks at the babies, showing she loves both children equally.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to one vocal skill. E.g. She would speak sadly.

c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.text: Explain how an actor playing the Narrator might use physicality in a scene where he warns the audience about fate, to create tension.
c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.marks:
Upper band (3-4): Detailed explanation of physical skills with justified effect. E.g. The Narrator could use a slow, deliberate gait to cross the stage, suggesting he is in no rush because fate is inevitable. Strong, upright posture with controlled gestures would communicate authority and control. He might make direct eye contact with the audience to break the fourth wall and make them complicit in the knowledge of what is coming. Tight, restrained muscle tension would contrast with the other characters’ emotional turmoil, showing his detachment.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to physicality. E.g. He would walk around the stage looking serious.

c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.text: Explain how a set designer could show historical and/or cultural context at one key moment in Blood Brothers. As part of your answer, roughly sketch an annotated design to help explain the layout of the set.
c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.marks:
Top band (7-8): Accomplished explanation of how set design communicates historical/cultural context. E.g. For the Skelmersdale relocation scene, the set could show a 1970s council estate with a playground, small gardens, and a bus stop — reflecting the real overspill estates built to move Liverpool families out of the slums. Faded red brick flats on the backdrop communicate working-class housing. Cultural context shown through a corner shop with period-appropriate signage and a milk float.
Mid band (4-6): Clear explanation with some historical/cultural detail.
Lower band (1-3): Limited explanation with little or no contextual understanding.

c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.text: As a sound designer, explain three sound effects you would use to show the social, historical or cultural context of Blood Brothers. Give examples from the performance text to justify your answer.
c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.marks:
1 mark for identified sound effect, to a maximum of 3 marks. 1 mark for linking to social/historical/cultural context, to a maximum of 3 marks.

Sound effects should demonstrate understanding of context.
• Factory machinery sounds — historical context of industrial Liverpool in the 1960s–70s.
• Beatles music playing on a radio — cultural context of 1960s Liverpool.
• Children playing in the street — social context of working-class neighbourhood life.
• Dole queue ambience / crowd murmuring — historical context of mass unemployment under Thatcher.
• Church bells — cultural/religious context of Catholic working-class Liverpool.

c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.text: As a director, identify the mood you want to communicate for one key moment in Blood Brothers. You must not use the closing scene/section. Explain how you would create the mood.
c0ce1fd6-d6b3-4cd6-a0bc-d1be4ca1e733.marks:
Top band (7-8): Accomplished explanation of how to create a specific mood using a range of directorial tools (blocking, pace, actor direction, design elements). Effective examples from the text.
Mid band (4-6): Clear explanation with some relevant examples.
Lower band (1-3): Limited explanation with basic reference to mood.
The mood must be identified and linked to a specific moment. The director should consider: how actors deliver lines, blocking and proxemics, lighting, sound, set, and costume choices.

ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.text: Name the musical form that has the structure AB.
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)

ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.text: State two features of ternary form.
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.marks: 1 mark for each valid feature, up to 2 marks. Possible answers: • It has three sections (ABA). • The opening A section returns at the end. • The middle B section provides contrast (e.g. different key, melody, dynamics). • It is sometimes called da capo form. • The return of A can be exact or varied.

ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.text: Describe how a composer creates contrast between sections A and B in binary or ternary form.
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.marks: 1 mark per valid point, up to 3 marks. Possible answers: • Introducing a new or different melody in section B. • Modulating to a different key (e.g. from the tonic to the dominant or relative minor). • Changing the dynamics (e.g. from forte to piano). • Changing the texture (e.g. from homophonic to thinner/polyphonic). • Using different rhythmic patterns. • Changing the tempo.

ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.text: Explain the difference between binary form and ternary form. Refer to the structure and use of sections in your answer.
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.marks: 4 marks. Possible answers: • Binary form has two sections (AB) while ternary form has three sections (ABA) (1 mark). • In binary form, the A section does not return after B (1 mark). • In ternary form, the A section returns after B, creating a sense of balance or completeness (1 mark). • Both forms use contrast between sections, but ternary has the added feature of recapping the opening material (1 mark). • Credit use of correct terminology such as modulation, da capo, tonic, dominant (1 mark).

ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.text: A piece of music begins with a lively melody in D major. A contrasting section follows in B minor with a different melody and quieter dynamics. The opening melody then returns in D major. Explain what form this piece is in and how you can tell. Use musical vocabulary in your answer.
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.marks: 6 marks across two levels. Upper band (4-6): Clearly identifies ternary form (ABA). Explains that the opening section returns after the contrasting middle section. Uses correct vocabulary (e.g. modulation, tonic, contrast, da capo). Identifies specific contrasting features: change of key from D major to B minor, quieter dynamics, different melody. Explains that the return of A creates balance. Lower band (1-3): Identifies ternary form but gives limited explanation. May describe some contrast but without precise vocabulary. May not clearly explain why the return of A is significant.

ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.text: Discuss the similarities and differences between binary form and ternary form. In your answer, refer to the structure, use of contrast, and how each form is used in different styles of music.
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
ff98d11e-2db8-4a5c-ab06-6a9155e68e67.marks: 8 marks. Top band (7-8): Thorough and detailed discussion. Clearly defines both forms (AB and ABA). Explains how contrast is created between sections in both forms (key, melody, dynamics, texture, rhythm). Explains the key difference — the return of A in ternary form. Gives examples of where each form is used (e.g. binary in Baroque dances, ternary in Classical minuets, Romantic piano pieces, or pop music). Uses accurate musical terminology throughout. Well-organised writing with clear communication. Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with mostly accurate detail. Defines both forms correctly. Describes some methods of contrast. Mentions at least one example or context for each form. Mostly accurate terminology. Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but lacks detail or accuracy. May confuse some features. Limited use of examples or terminology. Lower band (1-2): Basic awareness of the forms. May only describe one form or give vague or inaccurate information.

94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.text: Name the musical device where a melodic pattern is repeated at a higher or lower pitch.
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)

94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.text: State two differences between a pedal and a drone.
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.marks:
Award 1 mark per valid difference, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• A pedal is usually a single sustained/repeated note; a drone often involves two notes (tonic and dominant) (1).
• A pedal is typically shorter in duration and occurs within a section; a drone tends to last much longer, sometimes throughout an entire piece (1).
• A pedal usually has changing harmonies above it that may create dissonance; a drone provides a constant, unchanging sound bed (1).

94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.text: Describe how an ostinato is used in a piece of music you have studied.
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a clear description. Possible answers (e.g. referencing Africa by Toto or a Baroque ground bass):
• An ostinato is a short repeating pattern (1).
• In Toto's Africa, Riff b uses a five-note ostinato based on the pentatonic scale (1).
• It repeats over a sustained chord (C#m) in the introduction (1).
• The irregular groupings create syncopation that cuts across the 2/2 time signature (1).
Credit any valid studied example with accurate detail.

94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.text: Explain the difference between imitation and canon. Give an example of each in your answer.
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• In imitation, a musical idea is heard in one part and then copied closely but not exactly by another part (1).
• In canon, the melody is copied exactly, note for note (1).
• Valid example of imitation, e.g. fugues by Bach where the subject is altered slightly in subsequent entries (1).
• Valid example of canon, e.g. Pachelbel's Canon in D where three violin parts play the same melody entering at different times (1).

94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.text: A flute plays a two-bar pattern, then plays the same pattern again three notes higher. Name this device and say whether it is ascending or descending.
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.marks: 1 mark for: an ascending sequence. Accept sequence on its own for the mark; ascending is the detail that gains credit in a longer answer.

94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.text: Explain how the following musical devices are used in music from the Western Classical Tradition (1650–1910): sequence, pedal, and ostinato. In your answer, refer to their musical effect and give examples from specific eras where possible.
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
94800fa8-acb2-4914-8301-584445201e64.marks:
Top band (7-10): Thorough, detailed response covering all three devices with accurate musical vocabulary. Clear examples from specific eras. Explains the effect of each device convincingly.
Mid band (4-6): Sound understanding of at least two devices. Some use of musical vocabulary. At least one era-specific example. Some explanation of effect.
Lower band (1-3): Basic understanding of one or two devices. Limited musical vocabulary. Vague or no examples.
0 marks: No valid content.
Indicative content:
• Sequence: a melodic pattern repeated at a higher or lower pitch; used in Baroque music (e.g. Vivaldi) to extend ideas and build intensity; ascending sequences create excitement, descending sequences can create a sense of falling or sadness.
• Pedal: a sustained or repeated bass note (tonic or dominant) while harmonies change above; common in Baroque (e.g. tonic pedal in Vivaldi's Winter creates stillness); dominant pedals build tension before cadences in Classical and Romantic music.
• Ostinato: a short repeating pattern; Baroque ground bass is a type of ostinato; creates unity and drives the music forward; also appears in Romantic music to sustain mood.

f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.text: Identify the structure of a piece that follows the pattern ABACA.
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)

f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.text: State two ways in which a composer could vary the theme in a theme and variation piece.
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.marks:
1 marks for each valid way, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include any two of the following:
• Change the melody / add ornamentation
• Change the rhythm / tempo
• Change the key (e.g. major to minor)
• Change the dynamics
• Change the texture (e.g. homophonic to contrapuntal)
• Change the instrumentation / timbre
• Add chromaticism
• Change the accompaniment style

f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.text: Describe the structure of rondo form, explaining what happens in each section.
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The main theme (A) is heard at the start (1)
• Contrasting episodes (B, C, etc.) appear between returns of A (1)
• The A section returns each time, usually in the tonic key (1)
• The overall pattern is ABACA (or ABACADA for longer rondos) (1)
• The episodes provide contrast through changes in key, melody, dynamics, or texture (1)

f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.text: Explain how theme and variation form creates both unity and contrast. Refer to specific musical elements in your answer.
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Unity is created because every variation is based on the same original theme (1)
• The harmonic structure or melodic shape is often kept throughout (1)
• Contrast is created by changing elements such as melody, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, texture, key, or instrumentation (1 per valid element, max 2)
• For example, a variation might change from major to minor key, or add ornamentation to the melody (1)
• Credit specific era-related features, e.g. terraced dynamics in Baroque, rubato in Romantic (1)

f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.text: You are listening to an extract from the Classical era. Explain how the composer uses rondo form to create interest for the listener. You should refer to musical elements in your answer.
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.marks:
Indicative content (up to 6 marks):
• The A section presents a clear, memorable theme, often with balanced phrases and homophonic texture (1)
• The theme is likely in the tonic key with functional harmony and regular cadences (1)
• The B episode contrasts through a change of key (e.g. dominant or relative minor), different melodic material, or a change in dynamics/texture (1)
• The return of A creates familiarity and unity for the listener (1)
• The C episode provides further contrast, possibly with different instrumentation or a shift in mood (1)
• Classical features may include Alberti bass, clear phrase structures, and gradual dynamics (crescendo/diminuendo) (1)
• The recurring A section acts as an anchor, making the form easy to follow and satisfying (1)
Credit use of correct musical vocabulary and clear explanations of how elements create interest.

f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.text:
A movement is headed ‘Minuet and Trio’. The Minuet is played, then a contrasting Trio, then the Minuet again. Underline the structure of the movement.

Binary Ternary Rondo Theme and variations
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)
f5d8f6f1-327c-49bf-8183-6e33581f4dc5.marks: 1 mark for: Ternary (ABA). The Minuet is A, the Trio is B, and the Minuet returns.
